sections.heading: Seeing myself honestly and seeing your abundance
sections.text: Heavenly Father, you have shown me the truth about myself: left to myself, I am not a little broken but deeply sinful. And you have shown me the truth about you: you are overflowing with goodness. You have more than enough strength to help me, wisdom to lead me, mercy to make me alive, and love to satisfy the hunger of my heart.
theological_themes: Dependence on God's strength, wisdom, mercy, and love

scripture_references.connection: Paul's honest confession about the flesh gives biblical language for seeing the depth of sin in oneself without pretending it is small or manageable.
Paul prays that believers would be strengthened by God and know the vast love of Christ, which fits the prayer's confidence that God's strength and love are more than enough for the needy soul.

sections.heading: Receiving you as my life and strength
sections.text: Because you have given yourself to me, I do not have to live out of my own emptiness. Teach me to draw life from you, to stand in the strength you give, and to let your wisdom steady my mind and direct my steps. Let my thoughts and my heart settle down in you instead of scattering everywhere else.
theological_themes: Life with God as the source of spiritual strength
Depending on God rather than self
Resting the mind and heart in God

scripture_references.connection: Jesus teaches that fruitfulness comes from abiding in him, not from independent effort; this grounds the prayer's desire to live from God's life rather than self-sufficiency.
Paul says that the fullness of deity dwells in Christ and that believers have been filled in him, supporting the prayer's claim that God's fullness meets the believer's need.

sections.heading: The wonder that you give yourself to me
sections.text: Father, this love is almost too great for me to take in: you let me belong to you, and you give yourself to me. Everything good that I truly need is found in you. Even my coming to you was your grace at work, because I would never have come on my own. Now that you have brought me near, keep me close. Bind my heart to you, and keep me seeking you again and again.
theological_themes: God gives himself to his people
Grace draws the sinner to God

scripture_references.connection: Jesus teaches that no one comes to him unless the Father draws him, which directly supports the prayer's confession that even coming to God is the result of grace.
James calls God's people to draw near to God, matching the prayer's movement from being brought near by grace to actively clinging to and seeking God.

sections.heading: Choosing you above everything that fades
sections.text: There is no one good like you. With you, I can lose many other things and still not be ruined, because you are enough. The comfort, approval, pleasure, peace, and success this world offers can feel bright for a moment, but they are created things and they pass away. You do not. Teach me to want every good gift only in relation to you, and never as a replacement for you.
theological_themes: Contentment in God above created things
The passing nature of worldly satisfaction

scripture_references.connection: The psalmist confesses that God is his ultimate desire and lasting portion even when earthly strength fails, which closely matches the prayer's contrast between God and every lesser good.
John contrasts the passing desires of the world with the permanence of doing God's will, grounding the prayer's refusal to treat created pleasures as ultimate.

sections.heading: Wanting holiness because I want you
sections.text: Please convince me, deep down, that real hope is hoping in you, and receiving everything else only as something from your hand and for your purposes. Do not let me chase happiness apart from holiness. If I want to be full of your grace, then teach me to love what you love, turn from what grieves you, and find my joy in becoming more like Christ.
theological_themes: Holiness as the path of true happiness

scripture_references.connection: Hebrews connects the pursuit of holiness with seeing the Lord, showing that holiness is not optional decoration but belongs to the life of those who hope in God.
Paul describes grace not only as saving but also as training believers to renounce ungodliness and live for God, supporting the prayer's link between being filled with grace and growing in holiness.

sections.heading: Living now in the way I hope to die
sections.text: Father, do not let me comfort myself with empty words about heaven while refusing your will here and now. I know my obedience does not earn my place with Christ; only your grace can save me. But if I truly hope to be with Christ when I die, then make my life now show that I want him. Give me a sincere will to obey him, and let me taste his fullness while I am still living.
theological_themes: Death faced in hope of being with Christ
Present communion with Christ as preparation for eternity

scripture_references.connection: John treats obedience as evidence that a person truly knows Christ, not as a way to earn salvation; this helps clarify the prayer's concern for a real, not merely verbal, hope.
Paul speaks of death as being with Christ, which supports the prayer's longing to go to Christ while also living faithfully for him now.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original's final line could be misunderstood as making obedience the basis for peace at death or entrance to Christ. The adaptation preserves the warning that a professed hope without an intent to obey is hollow, while explicitly distinguishing evidence of genuine faith from earning salvation.
The phrase 'mass of sin' is intentionally severe Puritan language. The adaptation keeps its force as 'deeply sinful' and 'left to myself' without implying that the person is not made in God's image.
significant_interpretive_choices: The original speaks broadly of God's fullness, but the final reference to going to Christ and the biblical language of fullness led to expressing that fullness in relation to Christ where appropriate, especially in the sanctification and death sections.

The line about hoping for 'all things only for thee' was rendered as receiving every good gift from God and for his purposes, rather than rejecting created goods altogether. This keeps the original's God-centered aim without suggesting that creation itself is evil.
